newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major faces new blow over European Union.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major faces new blow over European Union.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major faced fresh revolt in his bitterly divided Conservative Party on Monday when one of its prominent "Eurosceptics" called for a referendum on Britain's European Union membership.
Maverick Conservative and ardent anti-European Teresa Gorman said she would introduce a bill in parliament next month calling for a plebiscite on whether Britain should stay in the EU.

By announcing the measure just one day after Major made a strong plea for party unity in the run-up to the next election, Gorman made clear that the prime minister could not expect hardline Eurosceptics to keep quiet over their number one concern.

Major, whose one-seat parliamentary majority vanished when a disaffected Conservative withdrew support last week over a hospital ward closure, vowed on Sunday he would not be held to ransom by "maverick" Eurosceptics intent on making trouble.
Gorman said she planned to press ahead with a bid to give Britons the option of pulling out of the European Union and she would introduce her bill on January 21.
"People on both sides of the political fence are frustrated because they are not being asked for their opinion. A referendum is essential to clear the air," Gorman said.
Eurosceptics are angered by what they see as an erosion of sovreignty by Brussels and want no further integration with the EU.

But Gorman and fellow Eurosceptic John Wilkinson said they had no plans to quit the Conservative Party because of their disapppointment over Major's reiteration of his "wait and see" policy on whether to join a single European currency.
Gorman will introduce the bill under the so-called 10-minute rule which gives MPs an opportunity to discuss matters of importance. But the bill has almost no chance of becoming law.
A referendum bill introduced earlier this year by another Conservative anti-European, Bill Cash, was supported by 78 members of the ruling party in parliament.

Both the Conservatives and the opposition Labour Party have pledged to hold a referendum on joining a single European currency after the next election -- which Major plans to call no later than May 1 -- but only if the cabinet and parliament first agree Britain should join.

Billionaire businessman Sir James Goldsmith, another prominent anti-European, has founded a single-issue political party which will fight the election on platform of offering Britons a referendum on ties with Europe.

Gorman said she had the support of seven other Eurosceptics who were thrown out of the Conservative parliamentary party in November 1994 for rebelling against government policy on links with the European Union.
Labour Party leader Tony Blair said Major's attempts to unite the Conservatives over Europe were already crumbling.
"It just isn't in the interests of the country to have a government stumbling, limping on with its factions simply tearing it apart," Blair said.
Opinion polls show the Conservatives as much as 37 points behind Labour.
The government is expected to be hit once again at a by-election on Thursday in Barnsley, in northern England, where Labour is widely expected to take the seat.
A parliamentary debate on the European Union starting on Wednesday will give Eurosceptics a fresh chance to air their grievances.
It will be followed by an EU summit in Dublin where other leaders will push for more European integration.
